paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Otters are semiaquatic (or, in the case of the sea otter, aquatic) mammals. They are members of the mustelid family, which includes badgers, polecats, martens, weasels, stoats and minks. They have inhabited Earth for the past 30 million years and, over time, their carnivorous bodies have undergone subtle changes that enable them to exploit the rich aquatic environment. Otters have long, slender bodies and short legs—ideal for pushing through dense undergrowth or hunting in tunnels. An adult male may be up to 4 feet long and weigh 30 pounds. Females are smaller, typically weighing around 16 pounds. The Eurasian otter’s nose is among the smallest of all otter species and has a characteristic shallow ‘W’ shape. An otter’s tail (or rudder, or stern) is stout at the base and tapers towards the tip, where it flattens. It forms part of the propulsion system when the animal swims quickly underwater. Otter fur consists of two types of hair: stout guard hairs, which form a waterproof outer covering, and dense, fine underfur, which acts as thermal underwear. The fur must be kept in good condition through grooming. Seawater reduces its waterproofing and insulating qualities when salt penetrates the fur. This is why freshwater pools are important to otters living on the coast. After swimming, they wash the salt off in the pools and then squirm on the ground, rubbing themselves dry against vegetation.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Scent is used for hunting on land, communication and detecting danger. An otter’s sense of smell is likely to be similar in sensitivity to a dog’s. Otters have small eyes and are probably short-sighted on land. However, they can modify the shape of the lens in the eye, making it more spherical and thereby overcoming the refraction of water. In clear water and good light, otters can hunt fish by sight. Their eyes and nostrils are placed high on the head so that they can see and breathe even when the rest of the body is submerged. Long whiskers around the muzzle detect the presence of fish by sensing the regular vibrations caused by a fish’s beating tail as it swims away. This allows otters to hunt even in very murky water. Underwater, an otter holds its legs against its body, except when steering, and flexes the rear of its body in a series of vertical undulations. River otters have webbing that extends along much of each digit, though not to the very end. Giant otters and sea otters have even more prominent webs, while the Asian short-clawed otter has none. The latter hunts for shrimps in ditches and paddy fields, so it does not need great swimming speed. Otters’ ears are protected by valves that close against water pressure.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Several constraints and preferences limit the habitats suitable for otters. Water is essential, and rivers must be large enough to support healthy fish populations. As shy and wary creatures, otters prefer territories where human activity does not intrude greatly. There must, of course, be no other otter already in residence—a consideration that has become significant again only recently as populations have begun to recover. A typical range for a male river otter might encompass 25 km of river; a female’s range is less than half that. River productivity has a major effect, however, and one study found male ranges varying from 12 to 80 km. Coastal otters have a much more abundant food supply, and the ranges of both males and females may cover only a few kilometres of coastline. Because male ranges are usually larger, one male’s range may overlap those of two or three females. Otters will eat almost anything they can catch; there are records of them gobbling sparrows, snakes and slugs. Apart from fish, their most common prey include crayfish, crabs and water birds. Small mammals are taken occasionally, most commonly rabbits but sometimes even moles.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Eurasian otters will breed at any time when food is readily available. In places with more severe conditions, such as Sweden, where lakes are frozen for much of the winter, cubs are born in spring. This ensures that they are well grown before severe weather returns. In the Shetland Islands, cubs are born in summer, when fish are more abundant. Although otters can breed every year, some do not; again, this depends on food availability. Other factors, such as food range and the condition of the female, may also have an effect. Gestation in the Eurasian otter lasts 63 days, except in the North American river otter, whose embryos may undergo delayed implantation.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Otters normally give birth in secure dens to avoid disturbance. Nests are lined with bedding—reeds, waterside plants and grass—to keep the cubs warm while their mother is away feeding. Litter size varies from one to five, with two or three being most common. For an unknown reason, coastal otters tend to produce smaller litters. At five weeks, the cubs open their eyes; at this stage, each tiny cub weighs about 700 g. At seven weeks, they are weaned onto solid food. At ten weeks, they leave the nest and blink in daylight for the first time. After three months, they finally enter the water and learn to swim. By eight months, they are hunting, although their mother still provides much of their food. Finally, after nine months, she can chase them away with a clear conscience and relax—until the next male appears.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The plight of the British otter was recognised in the early 1960s, but the chief cause was not discovered until the late 1970s. Pesticides such as dieldrin and aldrin were first used in agriculture and other industries in 1955. These chemicals are highly persistent and had already been identified as the cause of huge declines in populations of peregrine falcons, sparrowhawks and other predators. The pesticides entered river systems and the food chain—first microorganisms, then fish and finally otters—with each step increasing their concentration. The chemicals were phased out from 1962, but while some species recovered quickly, otter numbers did not; they continued to fall into the 1980s. This was probably due mainly to habitat destruction and road deaths. In populations fragmented by the sudden decline of the 1950s and 1960s, the loss of only a handful of otters in one area can make an entire population unviable and spell its end.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Otter numbers are recovering throughout Britain. Populations are growing in the few areas where they survived and have expanded from those areas into the rest of the country. This is almost entirely due to legislation and conservation efforts, which have slowed and reversed the destruction of suitable otter habitat, as well as to reintroductions from captive-breeding programmes. Many regard releasing captive-bred otters as a last resort. The argument is that where suitable habitat is absent, the animals will not survive after release, and where suitable habitat exists, natural populations should be able to expand into the area. However, reintroducing animals into a fragmented and fragile population may provide just enough impetus for it to stabilise and expand rather than die out. This is what the Otter Trust accomplished in Norfolk, where the otter population may have fallen to as few as twenty animals at the beginning of the 1980s. The Otter Trust has now ended its captive-breeding programme entirely—excellent news, because the programme is no longer needed.
